summary: Describes how to benchmark devices that forward MPLS packets, covering the most common forwarding scenarios and delay measurements for IP flows. It builds on earlier benchmarking work such as RFC 2544 and RFC 1242. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo gives a procedure for measuring how quickly a router forwards packets that carry MPLS labels. It sets out the equipment, the frame sizes and the tests, so that measurements from different devices can be compared.

subtitle: A repeatable way to measure how fast a device forwards labelled packets.

tldr.problem: There is no standard way to compare the packet forwarding performance of network devices when they forward MPLS packets.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a laboratory topology, the frame formats and sizes to use, and a set of tests for throughput, latency, frame loss, recovery and reset, built on the general benchmarking methodology of RFC 2544.
tldr.outcome: Five forwarding operations are measured separately, including three kinds of label pop, and the results are reported against a fixed list of parameters so that different vendors' numbers can be compared.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
MPLS, defined in RFC 3031, has seen increased use as a forwarding architecture in new and existing network designs. It is a foundation technology and the basis for many advanced ones, such as Layer 3 MPLS VPNs, Layer 2 MPLS VPNs and MPLS Traffic Engineering. There is, however, no standard method for comparing the foundational MPLS packet forwarding capabilities of network devices, and this document proposes a methodology using common criteria such as throughput, latency, frame-loss rate, system recovery and reset.

The benchmarking principles in RFC 2544 are independent of forwarding technique, but they do not fully address MPLS, because the load that MPLS forwarding places on the resources of a network device differs from that of IP forwarding. The methods here are limited to the most common MPLS packet forwarding scenarios in a laboratory setting, and build on the tenets of RFC 2544 and RFC 1242 along with other work of the IETF Benchmarking Methodology Working Group. It is a complement to RFC 2544, not a replacement.

The document focuses on an MPLS label stack with a single entry, because that is the basis of MPLS forwarding, and expects later documents to cover applications such as Layer 3 VPN, Layer 2 VPN and Fast ReRoute, which need more than one entry. It also uses IP packets as the MPLS payload, so that label distribution for IP forwarding equivalence classes is prescribed, and expects later documents to cover non-IP payloads. The presence of a label stack does not require the length of the payload to change, so the effective maximum size of a frame can increase by Z octets, where Z is four times the number of label stack entries.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS forwarding is different enough from IP forwarding that the usual test method does not cover it. This memo extends that method to the three label operations a router performs and says exactly what to measure.

sections.title: Test Topology and Conditions
sections.content:
The topology places the device under test between the transmit and receive sides of a test tool, with ports A1 to Ap on the transmit side and B1 to Bp on the receive side, and the device's own receive ports DA and transmit ports DB between them. The number of port pairs p is set by the maximum unidirectional forwarding throughput of the device and the load capacity of the port media: if the device forwards 100 frames per second and a single port carries 50, then at least two port pairs are needed. The exact throughput is a measured quantity that varies with the number of ports and other factors, and the number of ports used should be reported.

The methodology assumes a full-duplex, uniform medium, and the medium used must be reported in each result. Mixed media, speed mismatches and header differences are not considered, and features that affect traffic, such as flow control, quality of service and graceful restart, must be disabled unless the test case asks for them, as must any non-essential traffic.

It is recommended that all ports support a dynamic interior gateway protocol such as IS-IS, OSPF or RIP, and that the device be able to hold a stable control plane under heavy forwarding load, following the procedures of Section 11.3 of RFC 2544, so that control-plane instability is not what limits forwarding performance. The route distribution method used must be reported, as must any configuration used to keep the control plane stable.

The device and the test tool must support at least one protocol for exchanging MPLS label and forwarding-equivalence-class bindings, and must be able to learn and advertise those bindings and use them during forwarding all the time, including when the bindings change. The most common protocols are LDP, RSVP-TE and BGP, and all ports should support them for IPv4 or IPv6 forwarding equivalence classes. Static labels should not be used to establish the label switched paths, because static labels are uncommon in production networks. The IPv4 and IPv6 explicit NULL labels, values 0 and 2, are not used, because the tests are limited to one non-reserved label in the stack of every packet.

Further conditions are set out for the run itself. The time to live value must be large enough for a decrement to happen and for the packet still to be forwarded, and if the decrement is configurable its setting should be reported. Unless stated otherwise, the test portion of each trial should be at least 30 seconds with static routing and at least 200 seconds with a dynamic routing protocol and LDP, because the default LDP holddown timer is 180 seconds; the longer trial checks that the control plane stays stable while the forwarding plane is under stress. All traffic sent must be accounted for, whether it arrived on the wrong port, the right port or not at all, and the presence or absence of the label stack, every field in it, the ethertype, frame sequencing and the frame check sequence must be verified. All state for any dynamic protocol used must be established before the traffic starts.
sections.plainLanguage: The device sits in the middle of a traffic generator and a traffic receiver, and both ends exchange routes and label bindings with it so that the labels in flight are real ones. Everything else, such as graceful restart, is switched off so that the measurement is of forwarding alone.

sections.title: Frame Formats and Frame Sizes
sections.content:
A test frame carrying an IP packet has a Layer 2 header, an IP header and a UDP header, which is the frame format RFC 2544 prescribes. A frame carrying an MPLS packet adds an MPLS label stack immediately after the Layer 2 header and before the IP header. The label stack is a sequence of label stack entries, each four octets long, and this document requires exactly one entry. Label values used in any test case must be outside the reserved range 0 to 15 unless stated otherwise.

IP is the required Layer 3 protocol and the MPLS payload, for three reasons: it allows the use of IP forwarding equivalence classes, which every MPLS network needs; it provides a baseline for later benchmarking of applications such as Layer 3 VPN, Layer 2 VPN and traffic engineering fast reroute; and it lets the work build on RFC 2544, which uses IP packets with UDP data as test frames.

The frame format changes with the forwarding operation. In a label push, or LSP ingress, the device receives a frame with an IP packet and forwards a frame with an MPLS packet. In a label swap it receives an MPLS packet and forwards an MPLS packet. In a label pop, or LSP egress, it receives an MPLS packet and forwards an IP packet. The test tool therefore sends and receives the matching format for each case.

Because the label stack is assumed to be transparent to the IP layer, the effective maximum frame payload size is Z octets larger than the conventional maximum, where Z is four times the number of entries in the stack. Here the stack depth is one, so Z is 4 octets, and the media MTU value should be set to the effective maximum so that frames carrying MPLS packets are delivered successfully. On Ethernet, the frame sizes to use when the test tool sends or receives a frame carrying an IP packet are 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 1280 and 1518 octets. When it sends or receives a frame carrying an MPLS packet, four more octets are needed for the MPLS header, giving 68, 132, 260, 516, 1028, 1284 and 1522 octets. The 64 and 1518 octet sizes are the minimum and maximum length of an untagged Ethernet frame, and in operational environments a frame commonly ranges from 68 to 1522 octets, the minimum and maximum of a single VLAN-tagged frame. Jumbo frames are outside the 802.3 standard, but tests should use the sizes the device supports; common jumbo sizes are 4096, 8192 and 9216 octets. On packet over SONET media, where the Layer 2 header is about four octets, the label push sizes are 47, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 1280, 1518, 2048 and 4096 octets, and the label swap and pop sizes are 51, 68, 132, 260, 516, 1028, 1284, 1522, 2052 and 4100 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: The frame grows by four bytes when a label is added, so the test sizes for labelled frames are four larger than the plain IP ones. If the device will not accept the larger media MTU, the test cannot measure the true maximum and that has to be reported.

sections.title: The Benchmarking Tests
sections.content:
MPLS is a different forwarding paradigm from IP: a packet may carry more than one MPLS header and may pass through a push, a swap or a pop, so the benchmarking needs more granularity than RFC 2544 provides. The categories considered here are throughput, latency, frame-loss rate, system recovery and reset. The document focuses on the first five, in the spirit of RFC 2544, and leaves the MPLS traffic class field, negative scenarios such as time-to-live expiry, and multicast for elsewhere.

The test setup uses a single port pair where possible. If the device can forward faster than one port can carry, the extra ports must be enabled, first those that can together exceed the device's throughput without overloading a receive port and then all of them if that is not enough, following the multi-port procedures of Section 16 of RFC 2544. The test tool must not advertise a prefix to the device on more than one port, so that each forwarding equivalence class maps to exactly one receive port, and equal-cost multipath is not permitted, because its heuristics would make the forwarding behaviour non-deterministic.

The procedure sends traffic from the transmit ports at a constant load for a fixed interval and receives it on the receive ports. If any frame loss is detected, a new iteration lowers the offered load, and an iterative search finds the maximum offered frame rate with zero frame loss. That rate is the throughput as defined in RFC 2544, informally the no-drop rate.

Throughput is measured for five forwarding operations. Label push covers IP to MPLS. Label swap covers MPLS to MPLS. Label pop is measured three times: with an unlabeled outgoing label, with an aggregate outgoing label that covers a set of prefixes learned on the receive ports, and with penultimate hop popping, where the outgoing label is the reserved value 3. In each case the setup differs in which side the tool advertises prefixes and label bindings on, and in what the tool expects to receive back.

Latency measurement gives the average delay the device adds while forwarding a labelled packet, for each of the five operations. Frame-loss rate measurement gives the percentage of frames not forwarded under overload across a range of input rates and frame sizes; a frame received on the wrong port counts as lost, as does one with the wrong MPLS label. System recovery characterises how quickly the device recovers from an overload, and reset characterises how quickly it recovers from a device or software reset, with static routes and static labels in place of the dynamic protocols and all graceful restart features disabled. The reset procedures themselves are not specified here and are left to a separate document.

For each test case the report should give the forwarding equivalence class, the label distribution protocol, the MPLS forwarding operation, the interior gateway protocol, the throughput in frames and bits per second, the port media and speed, the interface encapsulation, the frame size and the number of port pairs.
sections.plainLanguage: Each test drives traffic at a fixed load and lowers it until nothing is dropped; the highest load that loses nothing is the throughput. The same runs are repeated for pushing a label, swapping one, and popping one in three different ways, and for delay, loss, recovery and reset.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The benchmarking described here is limited to technology characterization using controlled stimuli in a laboratory, with dedicated address space and the constraints set out in the document. The benchmarking topology is an independent test setup and must not be connected to devices that could forward test traffic into a production network or misroute traffic to the test management network.

Benchmarking is performed on a black-box basis, relying only on measurements observable from outside the device under test. Special capabilities should not exist in the device specifically for benchmarking purposes, and any implications for network security arising from the device should be the same in the lab and in production. The document says there are no other security considerations within its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The test network must not touch a production network, and the device must not have special hooks that exist only to make benchmarking easier, because then the lab result would not say much about the real one.
